Pregnancy

Swelling in pregnancy: what is common and what needs urgent care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Gradual swelling is common in pregnancy, especially in the feet and ankles. Sudden swelling, a painful swollen leg or swelling with other symptoms needs a different response: prompt assessment rather than reassurance based on how common oedema is.

Check for urgent symptoms before trying home care

Contact your maternity team immediately for a sudden increase in swelling of the face, hands or feet, especially with a severe or persistent headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, pain under the ribs, vomiting or feeling very unwell. Heartburn that does not settle with usual treatment can also deserve assessment. Do not wait to measure your blood pressure before calling.

A newly swollen, painful, warm or discoloured leg needs prompt assessment for a clot, particularly when one side is affected. Sudden unexplained breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or collapse is an emergency. These symptoms need assessment during pregnancy and after birth, rather than a trial of extra water or putting the feet up.

Why the body holds more fluid in pregnancy

Blood volume and total body water increase to support the placenta, the growing baby and changes in maternal organs. Plasma, the liquid part of blood, expands substantially. Fluid is distributed within cells and in the spaces around them, supporting circulation, oxygen and nutrient transport and removal of waste.

Descriptions sometimes quote several extra litres of body water or a plasma-volume increase of around 40–50% near late pregnancy. Individual changes vary, and these figures do not tell you how much to drink or whether swelling is harmless. Pressure from the growing uterus can also slow blood returning from the legs, allowing more fluid to collect in dependent tissues.

What uncomplicated swelling often looks like

Gradual swelling of both feet and ankles is common, particularly later in pregnancy. Fingers may also feel fuller and rings or shoes can become tight. Heat, humidity, standing for a long time and the end of the day can make fluid pooling more noticeable.

Not everyone develops visible swelling, and its amount does not measure how healthy the pregnancy is. Mild swelling that improves with rest is often uncomplicated, but a new pattern or other symptoms changes the assessment. Having a growing abdomen at the same time does not prove that swelling is normal. If a ring is becoming tight, remove it before it is difficult to take off.

Make movement and rest more comfortable

Take breaks from prolonged standing and rest with your feet raised when practical. Comfortable, supportive shoes and socks without tight bands can reduce pressure on swollen feet. Avoid spending long periods in excessive heat, and change position regularly rather than remaining seated or standing all day.

Gentle walking and ankle movements, such as bending, stretching and rotating the feet, may help circulation if your maternity team has not advised otherwise. A clinician may recommend properly fitted compression stockings, including for some long journeys. Ordinary tight socks are not the same. New one-sided painful swelling should be assessed before it is treated as a routine circulation problem.

Food and fluids support comfort, but do not diagnose or cure swelling

Drink regularly to avoid dehydration, following any individual fluid advice. Forcing large amounts of water does not reliably “flush out” oedema, and restricting fluids on your own can also be harmful. Sodium influences fluid balance, but pregnancy swelling should not be reduced to a judgement about one salty meal.

A balanced diet with fewer heavily salted processed foods can support general health. Bananas, avocado and other potassium-containing foods can be part of that diet, but they are not prescribed diuretics or treatments for pre-eclampsia. Do not start potassium supplements, water tablets or extreme salt restriction to remove swelling. NICE does not recommend salt restriction solely to prevent pregnancy hypertension or pre-eclampsia.

Pre-eclampsia is more than swollen feet

Pre-eclampsia usually develops after 20 weeks and can first appear after delivery. It involves new high blood pressure with other findings, such as protein in the urine or evidence that organs or the placenta are affected. Swelling can be a warning symptom, but it is not required for the diagnosis.

Protein in the urine is not present in every case. Blood tests may show liver changes or low platelets, and assessment can include kidney function and the baby’s wellbeing. Pressing a finger into swollen skin and seeing a dent, called pitting oedema, cannot diagnose pre-eclampsia. It can occur with ordinary swelling too. Regular blood-pressure and urine checks matter because early disease may cause few noticeable symptoms.

Recognise changes that deserve reassessment

A rapid increase in swelling, particularly around the eyes or across the face and hands, should prompt contact with maternity care. Sudden weight gain can reflect fluid retention, but it is not diagnostic on its own. Headache, visual changes, upper abdominal pain or feeling unusually unwell add urgency.

Pre-eclampsia can have serious consequences, including seizures, stroke and problems affecting the liver, kidneys, blood clotting or fetal growth. Timely treatment and monitoring reduce risk. You do not need to panic or wait until every symptom is present: describe what has changed and follow the team’s advice about assessment.

Assess pre-eclampsia risk early

Relevant factors include previous pre-eclampsia or pregnancy hypertension, chronic high blood pressure, kidney disease, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, some autoimmune conditions and a multiple pregnancy. A first pregnancy, family history, higher body mass index, older maternal age or a long interval between pregnancies can also affect recommendations.

The thresholds and combinations differ between guidelines. For example, some use age 35 and others age 40 as a moderate-risk marker. Gestational diabetes should be discussed in the whole clinical assessment rather than automatically treated as identical to pre-existing diabetes. Population disparities affecting Black patients reflect racism and unequal social and healthcare conditions, not a biological property of race.

Prevention needs an individual plan

Low-dose aspirin can reduce pre-eclampsia risk for selected people, including some who have never had it before. Depending on local guidance, one high-risk factor or a combination of moderate-risk factors may justify a prescription. The maternity clinician should choose the dose, start date and duration; do not start aspirin yourself to treat swelling.

Vitamins C and E are not recommended solely to prevent pre-eclampsia. Their antioxidant properties do not establish a clinical benefit. Keep taking supplements prescribed for other reasons, and ask before adding high doses. Appropriate physical activity supports general health, but exercise cannot guarantee prevention, and routine bed rest is not a preventive treatment. Attend screening even when you feel well.

Why a swollen leg may be a clot

A deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is a clot in a deep vein, often in the leg or pelvis. Pregnancy changes clotting and blood flow, and the risk remains raised after birth. CDC describes increased risk during the first three postpartum months, with the period soon after delivery particularly important.

A DVT commonly affects one leg and may cause swelling, heaviness, tenderness, warmth or discolouration. You do not need every sign or severe pain to have a clot. A piece can travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism. Assessment may include an ultrasound, and treatment may be started while tests are arranged if suspicion is high. Do not massage or exercise a painful swollen leg as a way to test whether it improves.

Clot prevention is separate from aspirin for pre-eclampsia

Tell your team about previous clots, close relatives with clots or a known thrombophilia. Reduced mobility, a hospital admission, surgery or caesarean birth, dehydration, certain pregnancy complications and conditions such as heart or lung disease can change the plan. Diabetes and other long-term conditions should be included in the medical history rather than treated as a stand-alone prediction.

For ordinary prevention, keep mobile as advised, move the legs during long periods of sitting and avoid dehydration. Ask about long journeys and compression stockings if relevant. People at higher risk may need prescribed anticoagulant injections, commonly low-molecular-weight heparin. Aspirin used for pre-eclampsia prevention does not substitute for this assessment or treatment. Do not add or stop either medicine without advice.

Continue to pay attention after delivery

Fluid shifts can make swelling noticeable after birth too, but that does not make all postpartum swelling harmless. Pre-eclampsia can begin after an apparently uncomplicated pregnancy, and clot risk continues beyond the first few days. Use the same urgent symptom checks rather than waiting for a routine postnatal visit.

For swelling assessed as uncomplicated, comfort measures and time may help. Ask what improvement to expect and when to return if the pattern persists or changes. Keep the maternity contact number available and tell any urgent-care clinician how recently you gave birth. The useful distinction is between an assessed, gradual pattern and a new or concerning change, not simply whether swelling is common.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Swelling alone neither confirms nor excludes pre-eclampsia or a clot.

Aspirin prevention and anticoagulant prevention address different risks and need individual prescribing.

How BeMama can help

Note when swelling began, whether one or both sides are affected and any accompanying symptoms before contacting maternity care.

When to seek help

Seek immediate maternity advice for sudden swelling, severe headache, visual changes or upper abdominal pain. Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or collapse needs emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Gradual bilateral swelling is common but not universal.
  • Body-fluid estimates are not drinking targets.
  • Pitting oedema is not a diagnostic home test.
  • Low-dose aspirin may be appropriate without a prior pre-eclampsia history.
  • Watch for pre-eclampsia and clot symptoms after birth too.

Frequently asked questions

Does every pregnant person get swollen feet?

No. Swelling varies, and having little or none is not a problem. A new or concerning change matters more than comparison with someone else’s pregnancy.

Is swelling in both legs always harmless?

No. It is a common pattern of ordinary pregnancy swelling, but sudden worsening or other symptoms still needs assessment. The pattern alone cannot rule out illness.

Does a dent after pressing the skin mean pre-eclampsia?

No. Pitting can occur with uncomplicated oedema and cannot diagnose the cause. Blood pressure, symptoms, urine and sometimes blood tests guide assessment.

Can pre-eclampsia occur without protein in the urine?

Yes. High blood pressure with other organ or placental findings can meet the diagnostic criteria. Do not use a past normal urine result to dismiss new symptoms.

Should I drink extra litres to flush the swelling out?

No. Keep normally hydrated and follow individual advice. Forced excess water is not a treatment, and the additional water held during pregnancy is not a recommended drinking amount.

Will bananas or potassium tablets act as a safe water tablet?

Potassium-containing foods can be part of a balanced diet, but they do not treat the cause of swelling. Do not take potassium supplements or diuretics for this purpose without a prescription.

Is aspirin only for people with previous pre-eclampsia?

No. Other high-risk factors or combinations of moderate risks may justify it. Ask your maternity clinician; the dose and timing should follow your local care plan.

Do vitamins C and E prevent pre-eclampsia?

They are not recommended solely for that purpose. Do not add high-dose antioxidant supplements as prevention, and continue supplements prescribed for a separate reason unless advised otherwise.

Can I wait to see whether a painful swollen leg settles?

New one-sided swelling, warmth, tenderness or discolouration needs prompt assessment for a clot. Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or collapse requires emergency help.

Does the risk end as soon as the baby is born?

No. Pre-eclampsia can first appear postpartum, and clot risk remains increased for the first three months. Tell urgent-care staff when you gave birth.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
